extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students (attending Ruskin's lecture on reading, education, and women's rôle)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the purpose of reading and education: what kinds of books to choose, why we read (moral and intellectual ends), how reading should shape character and social life, and the special relation of female education to social duty. Also prescriptive notes on public provision of books and libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reading — aim at kingly moral and intellectual power
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and literature are only useful so far as they tend to confirm calm, beneficent, and therefore kingly power — first over ourselves, and, through ourselves, over all around us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin insists the primary end of reading is moral formation: to produce a 'stronger moral state, and a truer thoughtful state' that enables one to guide and raise others. Reading should not be mere amusement; it should cultivate 'moveless' stability of character (state) and a capacity for useful influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why to read — to consult the wisest minds when our thought fails
rubrics_metrics.description: The first use of education was to enable us to consult with the wisest and greatest men on all points of earnest difficulty; to use books rightly is to go to them for help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading is an appeal to the united sentence of the judges and councils of all time against our solitary and unstable opinion. Use books as guides when personal knowledge or judgment is insufficient; reading should broaden sight and purify conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading should cultivate compassion and true action, not theatrical piety
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature and education should foster genuine compassion and practical Christian righteousness rather than 'dramatic Christianity'—a theatrical, decorative religion without true action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin contrasts gas-lit, ornamental religion with 'looking after Lazarus at the doorstep.' An anti-pattern is confusing religious ceremony or sentiment with moral duty; good reading promotes helping hands and plain deeds over sentimental show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select books that form a 'royal series' — the best in every kind for national libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: He hopes for royal or national libraries in every city, with a royal series of books in them; the same series in every library, chosen books, the best in every kind, prepared for that national series in the most perfect way possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prescription for curating collections: choose exemplary works across genres and standardise a high-quality canon for public access. The selection should be deliberate and represent 'the best' in each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical book design and binding standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts should be printed all on leaves of equal size, broad of margin, and divided into pleasant volumes, light in the hand, beautiful, and strong, and thorough as examples of binders' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin prescribes material quality as part of literary cultivation: books should be pleasant to handle and durable. Design and production are part of how books promote reading and respect for literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public library accessibility and conduct rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Great libraries should be accessible to all clean and orderly persons at all times of the day and evening; strict law being enforced for this cleanliness and quietness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules: libraries must be open widely but require enforcement of decorum so that they serve as true reading-rooms. Access coupled with orderliness supports useful reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusement should grow out of work; literature should replace false emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: When men are rightly occupied, their amusement grows out of their work; having no true business, we pour energy into false business and must have false emotions dressed up for us to play with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin criticises literature and spectacle that substitute manufactured sentiment for genuine feeling. As a criterion for evaluating works or cultural life, prefer works that foster emotions rooted in labor, compassion, and usefulness rather than sensational or mimetic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should teach ordinary habits of thought — combat childish illiterateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Many national faults resolve into conditions of childish illiterateness and want of education in the most ordinary habits of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful education is measured by its effect on everyday thinking skills — sobriety, deliberation, and teachability — not merely by erudition or technical skill. Anti-pattern: producing people of 'unreachable schoolboy’s recklessness' who acknowledge no master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and personal advancement — magnanimity as true advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: True advancement in life is to become 'mighty of heart, mighty of mind—“magnanimous”' — a person whose heart gets softer, whose blood grows warmer, whose brain quicker, whose spirit enters into Living peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal moral signs (increased compassion, warmth, quickness of mind, serenity) as criteria for judging real progress. Reject social advancement measured only by trappings, titles, or material gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women’s education — prepare for queenly power and public influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider what special portion of royal authority may rightly be possessed by women; education should fit them for a true queenly power—not merely in households but over all within their sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues education for women should cultivate the moral and intellectual qualities that enable them to guide and raise others. He rejects two errors: treating women as independent rivals of men, or as mere shadow/slave; instead education should form helpmates capable of effective counsel and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary standard for female characters — women as moral guides and redeemers
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare and Scott routinely present women as steadfast, wise counsellors, incorruptibly just and pure examples—often the agents of redemption where men's folly causes catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature (or composing characters), look for female figures who embody fidelity, wisdom, patience, and moral strength; note how tragedies are often caused by men's faults and redeemed, if at all, by women's wisdom. Anti-pattern: weak or passive female figures (e.g., Ophelia) who fail to guide and precipitate disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social relief and dignity — avoid insulting or painful forms of aid
rubrics_metrics.description: We make our relief either so insulting to the poor, or so painful, that they rather die than take it at our hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a standard for public charity, relief should not humiliate recipients; measures might include pensions at home or making relief comfortable. The goal is to preserve dignity and practical help rather than punish or stigmatise recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: National investment preference — spend on knowledge and culture rather than panic and war
rubrics_metrics.description: France and England buy panic of each other for millions annually; suppose instead they spent such sums founding royal libraries, art galleries, museums, and gardens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy rubric: nations should prioritise expenditure on cultural and intellectual infrastructure over militarised fear and spectacle. This is an argument for redirecting public capital toward institutions that cultivate mind and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of rule or dominion — count moral force not territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler's dominion should be estimated by the force of it (ability to say ‘Go’ and have men go, or ‘Come’ and have men come) — by multitudes influenced and degrees of love, not by miles of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating leadership or authority, prefer metrics of moral influence, love, and willing obedience over geographic or material measures. True kingship is ethical and relational rather than merely territorial.
